core_principles.text: Brace the core to maintain a neutral spine throughout the movement.
Lower the body with control until the chest approaches the floor.
Place the hands approximately shoulder-width apart.
Maintain a straight line from the head to the heels.
Press back to the starting position while maintaining alignment.

common_mistakes.text: Allowing excessive hip sagging during the movement.
Elevating the hips during the movement.
Adopting a forward-head posture during the movement.
Losing core engagement during the movement.
Allowing the trunk to collapse during the movement.
Excessive shoulder elevation during the movement.

consequences.text: Losing core engagement, sagging the hips, elevating the hips, or adopting a forward-head posture reduces exercise effectiveness and reinforces poor movement patterns.

core_principles.text: Proper technique helps target the intended muscles while maintaining efficient movement patterns.
Maintaining good alignment during push-ups helps reduce the likelihood of discomfort associated with poor movement mechanics.
Push-up difficulty can be adjusted by changing body position, leverage, stability demands, or training volume.
Incline push-ups allow beginner clients to develop strength and movement competency before progressing to more demanding versions.
Push-ups require upper-body strength, core stability, and the ability to maintain alignment under load.
Start in a plank position with hands positioned slightly wider than shoulder-width apart and feet together or hip-width apart.
Engage your core by drawing your navel toward your spine to maintain a straight line from head to heels and a neutral spine.
Lower your body toward the floor by bending your elbows, descending until your chest nearly touches the floor.
Keep your elbows at approximately 45 degrees from your body.
Press your body upward by extending your elbows, returning to the starting plank position without locking out your elbows at the top.
Descend until your chest nearly touches the floor or your elbows bend to approximately 90 degrees, whichever comes first based on mobility.

common_mistakes.text: Allowing the hips to sag during the movement.
Using jerky movements or excessive momentum.
Not achieving adequate range of motion.

specific_findings.text: Keep your elbows at approximately 45 degrees from your body.
Descend until your chest nearly touches the floor or your elbows bend to approximately 90 degrees.

consequences.text: Allowing the hips to sag indicates core disengagement and reduces exercise effectiveness.
Jerky movements or excessive momentum compromises form and reduces muscle engagement.
Flaring the elbows too wide increases shoulder stress and reduces chest activation.
Not achieving adequate range of motion limits chest stretch and development.
Excessive forward lean shifts emphasis to the shoulders and triceps.
Excessive depth during the descent compromises spinal alignment.

core_principles.text: Ideal alignment during a push-up requires that the kinetic chain checkpoints—ears, shoulders, hips, knees, and ankles—all remain in one straight line during both the descent and ascent.
If a push-up is too difficult to perform with proper form, it can be regressed by elevating the hands on a kitchen counter or wall to gradually progress the torso closer to the floor.

common_mistakes.text: Allowing the low back to arch or sag during the push-up as fatigue sets in.

consequences.text: Allowing the low back to arch or sag during a push-up decreases engagement of the deeper core stabilizers, increases involvement of the lumbar erectors, and increases stress on the vertebral discs.
Allowing kinetic chain checkpoints to migrate away from initial setup alignment due to fatigue causes unwanted muscular involvement and increased joint stress.

core_principles.text: Regress the push-up by placing the hands on a bench or the knees on the floor.
Progress the push-up by elevating the feet onto a box.

specific_findings.text: A specific progression for the push-up involves elevating the feet onto a 6-inch box.
